projects.name: Mau5head v2
projects.summary: This year's rebuild of my deadmau5 helmet: a clear PETG shell with LEDs glued into printed slots and lit tubes in the ears, 622 LEDs on one wire, with a show written for each of sixteen songs.

facts.Shell: Clear PETG, printed on a Prusa XL
facts.Lights: 622 WS2815 on one wire: 398 mapped in the shell (the print has slots for 948), 223 in the ears
facts.Controller: GLEDOPTO Elite running WLED, driven from a phone
facts.CAD: Parametric CadQuery model, edited in Onshape

details: Pixel pockets stop 0.8 mm short of the outer surface, so the shell diffuses each LED into a square dot
The visor hinges up on pivots hidden inside the shell, with a perforated mesh panel to see through
Ears are two-part prints lit by LED strips inside polycarbonate tubes, like a lightsaber blade
Shows are written for each song and run from a phone on the helmet's own Wi-Fi, with no laptop and no router
projects.writeup:
This page is the software side of the helmet. The hard parts were knowing where every LED physically is, keeping the thing cool enough to wear, making the lights land on the music, and running a whole show off a phone with no laptop and no Wi-Fi around.

I built most of this with Claude, over a lot of late nights. I decided what it should do and what looked wrong, and Claude wrote most of the code. The section on the songs says who did what, because that part is a good story.

Finding the LEDs

The print has a slot for every shell LED, 948 of them, plus three tubes and a rim channel in each ear. It can't tell you which LED went where. All of them hang off one data wire, and an LED's number is only how far along that wire it sits. The CAD lists the order I meant to wire the strips in, so the map had to find out what I actually built.

I started by hand: light each strip in turn and write down where it starts and stops. Then by camera: each LED lit alone in a dark room and photographed, and the centre of its glow recorded, one at a time. Two things went wrong. A reference LED, re-measured every so often to catch the camera getting bumped, kept appearing to jump 200 pixels. It hadn't moved. Its centroid was sometimes landing on a reflection, so now there are three references and a similarity fit. And a camera fitted to the shell came out at 0.000 px of error once the worst-fitting points had been dropped twice, because the survivors had walked onto one patch of the sphere. A flat set of points fits a camera exactly and tells you nothing about depth. There's a guard against that now.

The CAD's wiring order and the camera disagreed by about 15 pixels, so my first map slid each LED along the sphere until it sat on its own camera ray. That map then matched the camera to 0.02 px, which should have worried me, since a map built from a camera will always agree with it. From the front it looked right. From the side, LEDs near the edge had drifted as far as 113 mm, most of the shell sat between slots where no LED can be, and every ear LED had the same depth. I only caught it by turning the simulator side-on.

So the camera stopped placing anything. Every position now comes from the CAD, and the cameras only decide which slot each LED is in. That needed a second view, so I moved the camera up and to the right, about 34° from the first, and measured everything again. With nothing assumed about the helmet, the shell LEDs triangulate to a median of 173.3 mm from the centre of the head. The CAD's LED sphere is 173.0 mm, so the cameras could be trusted.

The chain then gets lined up against the CAD's wiring order with dynamic programming. Each LED is the next slot along its strip, or it skips an empty slot, or it starts the next strip from either end, and no slot can be used twice. A camera that sees an LED edge-on counts for less, because a glow at a grazing angle is clipped by its own recess and its centre shifts by 30 to 40 px. Both cameras get re-solved against the slots they picked, and it goes round again.

It converges from nothing but the CAD: 398 shell LEDs in 398 different slots, with exactly one slot empty, at the top of strip B04. Each camera run alone picks the same slot for all 398. Where a camera sees an LED square-on the error is 2 px. The strips beside the ear mounts turned out to be wired in a different order from my list, in the same mirror-image pattern on both sides.

Then I compared that with my notes from the first night. The cameras found 68 strips and so did the hand walk, and 67 of the boundaries are in the same place. The odd one out is a single LED among the two-LED strips at the chin. My notes already had all three surprises: the shell ending at LED 397, one strip with 11 LEDs instead of 12, and the mount strips out of order. The first map had overridden every one of them with the CAD's numbers.

The ears are where the cameras are weakest. They're only calibrated on the shell, and ear glows are wide and blurry. When I fitted each ear's position to its own LEDs, it matched a daylight photo worse than the CAD's position did. So the ears stay where the CAD puts them, and the cameras only pick where along which tube each LED sits: up and back along three tubes, then around the rim.

That second video is the original camera pass replayed, every centroid plotted as it was measured and in wiring order, so the faint line between dots is the wire. After that comes a flat bar swept down the helmet. It's the sharpest test of a map, because it only asks which LEDs light at the same moment, and diffusion can't blur that away.

The last six photos at the top of this page are the other passes. There's the supply ramped in steps until something gave, to find where the wiring really stops being stable. There's also the hunt for LEDs with a different colour order, which is a yes-or-no question (light a span red, see whether green comes back), so the search can halve each time. And the diagonal bands on the ears in the supply-ramp shot are the LED tubes showing through the diffuser. They got reported as "a line on the ears" and blamed on the map for a week. Every ear LED is lit in that photo, so the pattern is just where they physically are, and no software will even it out.

Effects are written against geometry

The helmet has no grid. It's a patch of sphere with a visor slot cut out of it and two discs on the sides, and all the strips are different lengths. There are no LEDs at all across the middle of the face. So an effect asks where an LED is: its height, its angle around the face, how far along its tube. There are 38 of them, from a plain colour wash to a spectrum analyser.

Text is the awkward case. Letters get rasterised into a small bitmap and sampled at each LED's position, because drawing them on a grid would bend them around the sphere. On this dome 27% of the cells contain no LED, so about a quarter of every letter used to vanish. Every lit cell that catches no LED now claims the nearest one.

Keeping it wearable

Full white on all of them is about 11.8 A, on somebody's head, in a glued-up shell with no airflow. The limit that matters here is heat, so the power model is a bucket of energy that leaks. The helmet can shed 11 W forever, and 7.4 W of that is just the LEDs idling. The bucket holds 3000 J of whatever goes above 11 W. Short hits can go up to 1 A of LED current, and as the bucket fills, the allowance eases down toward about 300 mA. My rule is that nothing stays raised for ten minutes or more, and that's a test in the repo: it checks the draw after ten minutes of worst-case content, and checks that delivered energy can never exceed what the helmet sheds in that time plus one bucketful.

Sizing the bucket surprised me. The obvious number was exactly ten minutes' worth of excess watts, and it broke the rule. Full-bright content starts near 25 W and the allowance eases down instead of stepping, so at ten minutes it was still drawing 14.3 W. The number had to be measured.

How a song becomes a show

The video at the top of this write-up runs through all sixteen. The first shows were automatic: analyse a track, pick effects by how loud each bar was. They followed the music, but they were just one effect after another. Tiki Tiki got its own world instead: an island at night, with an idol on the helmet. It was really good because it was unique, so I asked for more like it, each with its own idea.

Six shows came first, worked out back and forth between me and Claude: Strobe, its Dimension remix, Ghosts n Stuff, beneath, leavemealone and Tiki Tiki. The other ten got built on the day of a Halloween party. I wrote down everything we'd learned in one brief, gave each song a starting concept, and ran ten Claude sessions side by side, one song each. So those ten are first drafts. Nobody reviewed them before the party, and most had never run on the real helmet when they were finished. All of them compile and pass the checks.

Every show gets made the same way.

The beat grid gets measured first. A show is written in bars, so if the bars are wrong, everything is wrong. The automatic estimator regularly gets the tempo right and puts the bar line half a bar off, which ruins every drop. Tiki Tiki and the Nero remix were both half a bar off. The Veldt was off by about a beat. beneath shipped at 126.417 BPM when it's really 126, with a 122 outro, and that had the kick on the off-beat, one mark 251 ms late and another 214 ms early. So now somebody folds the audio onto the grid, looks at where the kicks and phrases really land, writes the grid out by hand, and checks it: worst reading under 15 ms wherever the music is clear.

Next comes the song's form. A script prints a bar map with a chord fingerprint for each bar, and there's a spectrogram tool. Each transition gets zoomed into, so a mark like "the kick comes in" sits on the bar where it actually comes in. The Veldt, for example: the kick enters on 8, leaves on 64, comes back on 72 and stops on 88.

Then you pick a world and give each part of the helmet a job, which is where most of the decisions are. There are three parts, and they're good at different things.

  • The ears are the instrument. Each one has three tubes and a rim, they can flash faster than the shell, and nobody reads them as a picture, so they play something in the music. In leavemealone they're the drums, kick on the rims and snare up the tubes. In The Veldt each new chord fires a tube, low chords the low tube. In Harder Better Faster Stronger they're a drum machine with one part per channel. I Remember goes the other way: they only breathe, and their colour is the chord.
  • The dome holds the picture. It resolves about 17 by 17 cells, and solid shapes read far better than outlines. Soft things read best, because the shell diffuses everything. So you get an idol's brow, a lion rising a row every two bars, a radio dial with a needle, a tiger.
  • The jaw is a thin arc at the bottom, cut off from the dome by the visor. It works as a strip: teeth, a conveyor belt, a film strip, an army marching, a magma pool that throbs on the kick, a voice box as wide as the voice is loud.

Then the parts of the song map onto those jobs. Breakdowns strip back to almost nothing, sometimes one thing moving in the dark. Builds have to visibly grow, like the pool in beneath rising up through the face. A motif comes back when the music does: Strobe's arpeggio is one constellation of sixteen sparks, and it returns whenever the arpeggio returns, including in the Dimension remix, which quotes it on purpose. A drop lands exactly on the bass, and usually the beat before it is dark, because contrast does most of the work.

Last comes the power guard, which runs on everything and changes how a show looks. The shell is capped near 300 mA, and when the whole frame hits 1 A the guard sheds the shell first, hard. So a big hit with loud ears can leave the shell almost black. Tiki's final hit at bar 153 sends 1000 mA with the shell at a mean of 2.2 out of 255 and the ears at 54.8. In the Dimension remix the snare's left and right halves went dark this way until the kick came down to under half and the snares to 0.6. The fix is usually to give a hit's first beat to one thing. The Veldt floods the shell with dark ears on bars 8, 48 and 72, and on bar 80 the ears blaze while the shell waits. Some Chords gives its flood to the shell and its one white moment to the ears.

The previews lied at first, too. The preview tool skipped the guard, so everything looked great, until the session working on the Radio Edit noticed its shell reading a mean of 90 where the guard would really allow about 10. Everything judged before that had to be judged again.

A few rules came out of all this:

  • The compiler refuses whole-shell flashing faster than 8th notes, because whole-shell flicker just reads as a fault. The ears can go faster.
  • Bright full-helmet white is for one moment in a song at most. Tiki saves it for bar 153, Animal Rights for bar 112, Some Chords for bar 164.
  • Words on the helmet are the song's title, never other lyrics, and usually only once. Harder Better Faster Stronger crosses its title words 36 times, since that's the whole song.
  • No power limit ever gets raised. If a scene runs too hot, it gets darker.

That last one is where the drafts still fall short. Played back to back in a long set, a show should average 11.5 W or less and never more than 12.5 W, or the bucket fills after 20 to 40 minutes and every hit after that gets flattened. Of the ten new ones, only Some Chords is under 11.5, and six are over 12.5. I Remember is the worst at 15.2 W.

The sixteen shows

SongThe ideaWhat the parts do

StrobeThe arpeggio is a constellation. 128 BPM.Sixteen sparks on the face, ice for the climb, dawn for the breakdowns, spinning rims and a blade ladder on the ears. White once, on the drop at 217. Its intro is really 176 BPM with no pulse after that until bar 125, and a 128 grid can't follow it.
Strobe (Dimension Remix)Strobe's language, at 174.The same sparks and palettes. The ears play the breakbeat, the snare hits one half of the shell and then the other, and the helmet goes dark for each one-beat hole in the bass.

Each generator script and its build notes are in tools/showkit/songs.

Everything stored about a song

People have been asking about this one. For each song there's an analysis file made once on the laptop and a compiled show, and no audio in either of them. Here's all of it, using The Veldt as the example. It's 170 seconds long, and its analysis file is 185 kB.

DataWhat it isHow it's madeUsed at playback?
beats, bars363 times and 91 times, in secondsMeasured by hand into a .beats file on 13 of the 16 songs. The other 3 still use the estimator.Yes. Every frame turns time into a bar.
bpm, lock128.007, and how sure the estimator wasA comb over the onset curve from 70 to 180 BPM, in steps of 0.0012 BPM, scored at 4 harmonics.Only when checking a grid.
bass, mid, high energy3 curves at 40 Hz, 0 to 1Mean log magnitude in 30 to 170, 170 to 2200 and 2200 to 10000 Hz, each scaled between its own 5th and 97th percentile for the song.Yes, where a scene asks. The Veldt has 5 such values, Tiki has 16, Some Chords has none.
bass, mid, high punch3 more curves: how hard the band just roseBand flux scaled to its 98th percentile, with a 100 ms tail.Yes, same as above.
energyOverall loudness at 40 Hz50 ms RMS in dB, scaled between the song's 5th and 97th percentile.By the fallback cue list. Scenes don't read it.
onsetHow much the spectrum just changedRectified spectral flux, minus a local mean. This is what the tempo search runs on.No. It's still saved and nothing reads it.
chroma12 numbers per bar, one for each noteSpectrum from 55 to 2000 Hz, binned by pitch class.By a few listening presets on the cue list. For scenes it's reading material while writing the show: it's how you spot a chord loop.
levels, sectionsEach bar ranked 0 to 3, grouped into runs of 8 to 24 barsRank of RMS, sub-200 Hz share and flux, split at the 30th, 60th and 85th percentile.Only to build the automatic cue list.
src stampThe MP3's size and SHA1Checked on load, so an analysis can't go with the wrong file.No.
scenes, hits, palettes22 scenes and 88 hits in bars, plus colour palettesWritten by a generator script for each song and compiled.Yes. This is the show.
sprites33 small pictures, as rows of textDrawn by hand as text.Yes.
holdsPlaces the beat counter stops, in beatsFound from gaps in the beat list.Yes. See the next section.

All of it gets computed from a mono copy at 22050 Hz, using a 1024-point FFT with a hop of 256, so a frame every 11.6 ms. The onset time has a 13.3 ms correction in it, measured against synthetic click tracks, because spectral flux peaks slightly after the real hit.

The controller is short on room. It has 983 kB of storage, and at the last deploy 839 kB was in use. So a song gets packed into a little drive file: the 7 curves as single bytes at 10 Hz (20 Hz for six of the songs), plus beats, bars and chroma. Punch curves keep each window's peak so a kick can't fall between samples. For The Veldt that's about 14 kB, and all 16 come to 564 kB gzipped. The page holding every show is 1.6 MB, or about 204 kB gzipped. If a drive file won't fit, it's skipped and the song plays without it, with its band values parked at the midpoint.

The song itself never goes on the controller, and I couldn't host it anyway. The MP3 goes into the phone's browser storage the first time, so the phone only needs a copy once.

How the lights stay on the music

The song is the clock. On the phone, every frame starts by asking the audio element for its currentTime, and the frame is worked out from that one number: time to beats with B = (t - t0) / spb, beats to bars, bars to which scene and hits are on. A scene frame depends only on the time and the band curves, so nothing drifts. Pausing holds one moment, and jumping costs nothing. Only effects that keep no state are allowed in scenes, and that's why.

Holds deal with songs that aren't perfectly straight. The formula above is a straight line, and real tracks sometimes aren't. Tiki Tiki has a splice at bar 119.5 where the music comes back 197 ms late, so the beat counter stops for 0.45 of a beat there and carries on. The Radio Edit has the same thing at bar 72, 32 ms late. beneath slows from 126 to 122 near the end, with 39 tiny holds. Raise Your Weapon uses about 500: it really speeds up from 128 to 140 over 16 bars, and holds can only delay, so 140 is the line and everything before it gets stopped a little at each beat. The grid written that way stays within about 5 ms of the real beats.

Whether a show follows its music is hard to judge by watching thirty seconds, so there's a scorer for it. Over one whole track it found the helmet's brightness correlating +0.02 with the music: the loud effects had landed in the quiet sections, because the heat budget was holding the show flat at its floor the entire time. Re-sizing the budget took the average from +0.23 to +0.43.

A frame goes from the show to the power guard to the controller. The phone caps at 30 frames a second and sends one at a time, so a slow link drops frames and never queues them up, and a late frame can't make the show fall behind. On WLED 16 it sends binary DDP packets over a WebSocket and gets about 24 to 27 fps. If a laptop tab gets covered, a worker keeps the clock running. If the socket goes silent for 6 seconds it's replaced. If a song fails to load, the set skips it.

One gap: nothing corrects for delay after the phone. The frame is drawn for right now and lands on the LEDs a little later, and a Bluetooth speaker plays the song later than the phone thinks. Each show has a lead setting that could shift the lights to match, but it's 0 on every one of them.

The live analysis

The shows above know the whole song in advance. There's a second mode for a song the helmet has never heard, like whatever you drop into the simulator. Then the listening effects, like the equaliser and the pulse, run on an analysis that happens in the browser as the song plays. The video runs the page's real code over one of my synth tracks, so the numbers on screen are what it actually got.

It uses two Web Audio analyser nodes on a timer, 50 times a second, separate from drawing, because the draw rate depends on the link and onsets sampled at 4 Hz aren't onsets. A short 1024-point window finds hits. A long 8192-point window finds pitch, because at 44.1 kHz the short one's bins are too wide to tell one semitone from the next.

Loudness has no reference, since the page has no idea how loud anything is in the room. So it keeps a running quiet mark and loud mark, and the reading is where you sit between them. The marks follow quickly when you go past them and relax slowly otherwise. Bass, mid and high use the same split as the offline analysis, with one of those for each band, since otherwise the top octave would never move next to the bass. Levels go up fast and down slowly, like a meter. Without that, the equaliser twitched between ticks and looked like a fault on the helmet. The first version also took a log of a spectrum that was already in dB, which flattened the loud bands and blew up the quiet ones. It now reads the real dB values, because the byte version clipped: in one test the bass bins sat at maximum for 23% of ticks through Strobe's drop.

A beat is a jump in the spectrum. Each tick adds up how much every bin between 40 Hz and 12 kHz rose since the last tick. That counts as a beat if it clears the mean plus 1.4 standard deviations of the last 5 seconds, it's above a fixed floor, and it's been at least 0.16 seconds since the last one.

The tempo comes from the last 24 beats. Every gap gets folded into one octave, 0.34 to 0.86 seconds, so a missed beat or an extra one lands in the same range, and it takes the median. It needs 6 beats before it says anything, and if the gaps disagree by more than 55% it keeps the old answer, because a wrong tempo is worse than none. Until then it assumes 120. In the video it reads 125 on a 124 BPM track, because it only looks every 20 ms and the gaps come in steps. Nobody had noticed that until it ran for this video.

Analysed ahead of timeLive
ScalingAgainst the whole songAgainst what it has heard so far
TempoComb over the whole song, then checked by handMedian gap of the last 24 beats
Beat positionA full grid of every beatRuns forward from the last thing it called a beat
BarsYes, with the bar line measuredNo idea
What's comingAll of it, so a build can lead into a dropNothing

So the song shows don't use the live path: a scene runs on its grid and the song clock, and the live mode gets the listening presets.

Where the sound comes from depends on the device. A file you pick plays through the analyser on its way to the speaker. A microphone needs a secure page, and the page on the controller is plain http, so navigator.mediaDevices doesn't exist there. Spotify gives you no audio at all, and its analysis endpoints are closed to new apps. So in Spotify mode the phone polls for the current song and position about once a second, and if it matches a show by name, the show runs on that position: it snaps if it's over 600 ms off, and otherwise eases 15% of the way each poll. It needs internet, so it can't work on the helmet's own Wi-Fi.

No laptop, no network

At a show there's no Wi-Fi worth trusting. The helmet brings up its own access point and serves the player page off the LED controller's own filesystem, so any phone works with nothing installed. That location is forced. A browser can't send UDP, an https page can't reach a plain http address on the local network, and a plain http page isn't a secure context, so a service worker can't cache it and a laptop can't serve it from somewhere else.

That meant porting the engine, the power guard and the show player to JavaScript. The tests render every effect in both languages and diff them, and the guard and the shows the same way. In the last run the worst difference across all 16 shows and 12,806 frames was 0.0005 of a count out of 255. Those show tests use synthetic music, so real band curves aren't covered by that number.

Running it against the real controller found four bugs that all failed the same way, by sending successfully and changing nothing. Writing pixels blanks the rest of the strip, so partial updates were showing a fifth of each frame. A WebSocket message that spans two TCP packets gets dropped silently. The firmware never acknowledged a pixel write, so pacing on acknowledgements pinned it at 4 fps. And the brightness limiter was being set on a key the firmware accepts and ignores. None of that shows up unless you read the strip back, so there's a tool that does.

About the videos

Everything with the helmet in the three new videos is simulated, using the real engine and power guard on the real LED map. The first night's footage and the preset photos in the other two are real.

The music is all made by a small synth in tools/film/score.py, since I can't host the songs. In the videos that show a song, it plays that song's measured beat grid and its bass, mid and high curves, with its own chords. So you're hearing the data the helmet has, played back.

Try it

The simulator runs the same engine, power guard and show player as the helmet, on this map, inside the helmet's CAD. Play your own song and the effects follow it live, or pick one of my shows and it plays to your copy of its song. The audio never leaves the page. The code is on GitHub.

projects.name: SAO MANY SAOs
projects.summary: A DEF CON 33 badge that powers and displays 25 SAOs at once. I designed it, had it made, tested every board, and sold it at DEF CON and through Hacker Warehouse.

facts.Power: 2 × 18650, charged over USB or barrel jack
facts.Lights: White ARGB edge LEDs, driven by the SmartAO

details: Every SAO port has a notch on the left for tying on a leash
Red and green LEDs next to the batteries show charging and full
If the badge is on while charging, the power goes to the SAOs instead of the cells
The kit included printed clips that add a leash ring to keyhole-style SAOs
SmartAO: a companion hex SAO with an RP2040, USB-C, and BOOT/RST buttons. It plugs into the top-left slot and runs the edge LED animations
projects.writeup:
I built SAO MANY SAOs because I had a simple problem: I'd collected a bunch of SAOs, and there was no good way to power and display them all at once. Most badges support one or two. I wanted something that could handle all of them at the same time without being fragile or just decorative.

Learning PCB design

When I started, I didn't know how to design a production-ready PCB at this scale. I learned by doing: watching tutorials, asking questions in Discord servers, and iterating quickly. A lot of the early work was figuring out how to route power safely across a large board and keep signals clean with that many connectors.

The layout was the hardest part. Supporting 25 SAOs meant thinking carefully about spacing, mechanical stress, and how people would plug things in without snapping headers. SAOs vary a lot in current draw, so the power design had to handle the worst case without failing.

Once I had a working design, I ordered prototypes and tested them with real SAOs, mixing high-draw and low-draw modules, checking voltage stability, and making sure everything behaved. I revised the design from that testing before the production run.

Production

I handled most of the assembly myself, with help soldering and prepping units. Every board was tested for power, charging, and SAO connections before it shipped. I was involved in every step, from PCB design to packaging, pricing, and getting badges into people's hands at DEF CON.

How it went

I shared it on Reddit and in the badgelife community. The response was really positive, especially from people who already owned lots of SAOs and never had a way to show them all at once. It pushed me to learn PCB design, power management, manufacturing constraints, and how to ship a real hardware product to real users.

projects.name: Mau5head v1
projects.summary: My first deadmau5 helmet: a 3D-printed head with sound-reactive WLED strips around the ears and mouth. Someone bought it for about $700.

facts.Parts: Six major pieces plus the mesh, joined with dovetails
facts.Finish: Primer, black, graphite powder, 2K clear coat

projects.writeup:
Lights

The lights run on a WLED controller I bought on Amazon for $30, with addressable RGB strips soldered to it. It's sound reactive because it has a small microphone, which works great as a wall display, but I couldn't get it to work well while walking around.

To power it I carried a 300 W Anker backup battery. I could have used something smaller, but I already owned it and didn't want to spend more. The controller and LEDs run at 12 V, so I used the battery's wall plug.

Printing

I printed it on a Prusa XL and my Bambu P1P, split into six major pieces plus the mesh. Dovetails made the joints easier, and I melted them together with a soldering iron and a little glue. The ears are lightweight PLA, attached with epoxy and two large bolts I had lying around.

Paint

After some sanding I used about one can of Duplicolor automotive primer, then black spray paint. On top of that I rubbed in graphite powder to make it silvery, which shows in the photos with more light, and locked it in with 2K clear coat.

Assembly

I got a hard hat for free from my neighborhood Facebook group, cut out the brim and sides with a Dremel, and cut two large rectangles so it could pass through the ear slots. I glued it in with two-part epoxy and epoxy putty, plus a lot of clamps and duct tape.

I sold it for roughly $700, which is why there's a version 2.

projects.name: Billet Mac Mini Case
projects.summary: A case machined from solid aluminum that doubles as the heatsink for a bare M4 Mac mini logic board. No fan, no stock power supply.

facts.Cooling: Passive. Fins on the lid, a pedestal touches the SoC
facts.Power in: XT60 on the back, 12.6 V DC

details: The board is stripped of its fan, power supply, and stock heatsink
The board mounts SoC-up and screws into the case; rear ports stay open

projects.name: Delta Printer Music
projects.summary: A Python G-code generator that plays songs on my delta printer's stepper motors, including chords and percussion hits.
details: Notes come from carriage speed: frequency ÷ steps per mm
Microstepping drops from 16× to 4× during playback for more volume
Percussion is a short, fast Z move; direction alternates so Z doesn't drift
Separate 10-second tuning files for each note, checked with a phone tuner

details: Pulls temperature, wind, and precipitation automatically; avalanche danger is set by hand
Picks a full layering stack in wear order, the best ski from my quiver, and head gear

Type any model name and it fills in the specs
